scene1_intro.title: The Channel Noise Paradox
scene1_intro.text: When information travels through physical copper or optical fiber, channel noise inevitably corrupts digital bits. A simple parity check computes the sum modulo two, but if two bits flip in transit, the parity remains identical—the error passes completely undetected. To construct an unforgeable defense against burst errors, we shift away from ordinary arithmetic into polynomial algebra. This is the Cyclic Redundancy Check.

scene2_mathTheory.title: Field Theory & Modulo-2 Arithmetic
scene2_mathTheory.text: At the foundation of CRC lies the Galois Field of two elements, GF(2). In this algebraic domain, addition and subtraction are completely identical, both collapsing into the exclusive OR operation. One plus one is zero. Zero minus one is one. There are no carries between columns and no borrows across digits. Long division under modulo two is not about numeric magnitude, but pattern matching: if the leading bit is a one, we XOR with our divisor. If it is zero, we XOR with seventeen zeros, shifting our window forward.

scene3_frameSetup.title: Structuring the Dividend & Degree-16 Generator
scene3_frameSetup.text: Consider our exact ten-bit payload from the laboratory: 1101011011. To protect these bits, we deploy CRC-CCITT, defined by the degree-sixteen polynomial x to the sixteenth plus x to the twelfth plus x to the fifth plus one. Written as a bit vector, this yields our seventeen-bit divisor: 10001000000100001. Because the polynomial degree is sixteen, we append exactly sixteen zeros to our original dataword. These sixteen appended slots represent the mathematical space where our checksum will be forged.

scene4_divisionWalkthrough.title: Sender Long Division Walkthrough
scene4_divisionWalkthrough.text: Observe the classic long division bracket. On the left is our seventeen-bit generator polynomial: 10001000000100001. Under the line sits our twenty-six-bit dividend: ten data bits followed by sixteen zeros. Look at our leading bit. It is a one. Because it is a one, the quotient receives a one, and we subtract our seventeen-bit generator. In modulo-two arithmetic, subtraction is bitwise XOR: one XOR one cancels to zero. We bring down the next bit from the dividend. The new leading bit is again a one. The quotient receives a one, and the generator subtracts again. On the third step, our leading bit is a zero. Because this bit is zero, the quotient receives a zero, and we subtract seventeen zeros. XORing with all zeros leaves every bit intact, shifting our working window forward. Step by step, bit by bit, the ladder cascades down. The original ten payload bits are drawn down, leaving behind a sixteen-bit remainder: 1011111011001101. This is our CRC checksum.

scene5_receiverValid.title: Receiver Verification: The Clean Invariant
scene5_receiverValid.text: At the receiving terminal, the twenty-six-bit codeword arrives intact. The receiver does not need to split the message and checksum. Instead, it feeds the entire concatenated sequence into the exact same generator polynomial. Because the checksum was constructed specifically as the mathematical remainder of this polynomial division, the incoming codeword is an exact algebraic multiple of the generator. Every single non-zero bit cancels out through the XOR chain. When the final bit drops into place, the remainder collapses entirely to sixteen zeros. The receiver confirms zero error.

scene6_receiverError.title: Detecting Corruption: The Non-Zero Syndrome
scene6_receiverError.text: Now observe what happens when noise corrupts the channel. A single bit at the tail flips from a one to a zero. As the receiver computes long division, this single discrepancy alters the downstream XOR calculations. When the division terminates, the remainder does not collapse to zero; it produces a non-zero syndrome: 0000000000000001. Instantly, without ever requesting the original message, the receiver recognizes the violation of polynomial invariance and rejects the packet.
